intro: A sum of neighbor features retains multiplicity that a mean can erase. A GIN-style layer combines that sum with a weighted self feature before applying a two-layer transformation.
task: Compute the neighbor sum and self contribution, then apply a two-layer MLP. Compare repeated neighbors with a single neighbor and inspect where the activation belongs.
signature: gin_layer(adjacency, features, w1, b1, w2, b2, epsilon=0.0)
requirements: features has nonempty shape (N,F). adjacency is a nonnegative (N,N) matrix with zero diagonal; adjacency[i,j] weights the message from node j to node i. It need not be symmetric.
w1 is (F,H), b1 is (H,), w2 is (H,O), and b2 is (O,), with H,O>0. epsilon is a finite real scalar and may be negative.
Compute combined=(1+epsilon)*features+adjacency@features, hidden=max(combined@w1+b1,0), and output=hidden@w2+b2. Return shape (N,O); there is no final ReLU or degree normalization.
Numeric inputs must be real and finite with magnitude at most 1e30, in addition to the bounds above. Leave all inputs unchanged and raise ValueError for invalid inputs.

hints.title: Do not average the neighbor messages
hints.body: Two identical neighbors contribute twice as much as one identical neighbor.

hints.title: Track both biases and the activation
hints.body: Only the hidden layer uses ReLU. Negative final outputs are valid.

explanation: The self coefficient 1+epsilon controls how the node’s own features enter the aggregate. The zero-diagonal contract prevents accidental double counting through the adjacency matrix.
Changing a sum to a mean removes neighborhood-count information. This lesson demonstrates the layer calculation; it does not claim every parameter choice distinguishes every pair of graphs.
Ported the upstream GIN sum-and-MLP equation to NumPy with explicit edge direction, supplied weights and strict shapes. Kept the final output linear and epsilon unrestricted in sign.
